01.actor: A man who held a betrothal feast, and Rava
01.event: A man prepared a betrothal feast on the ninetieth day after a woman's first husband died, and Rava made him forfeit the feast.
01.turn: The Gemara raises this as an objection, then answers that the feast was really a marriage feast.
01.outcome: The objection is dismissed: a betrothal feast would have been allowed, but this one was a marriage feast.
01.summary: A man once held a betrothal feast on the ninetieth day after a woman's first husband died. Rava made him lose the feast. The Gemara explains that it was in fact a marriage feast, which was why Rava forbade it.
01.missing: Who the man was and what happened to him after he lost the feast. The incident is only cited as an objection.

03.event: Rava Tosfa'a ruled a child fit when a woman's husband went overseas and her baby was delayed in the womb for twelve months.
03.turn: The Gemara asks whose opinion he followed, since it is a minority view.
03.outcome: The Gemara answers that he followed the majority, because Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel also holds a baby can be delayed.
03.summary: A woman's husband went overseas and she bore a child twelve months later. Rava Tosfa'a ruled the child fit and not a mamzer. The Gemara first asks how he could rely on the minority view of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, then explains that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel agrees, so he was following the majority.
03.missing: The woman's identity and what happened to her or the child afterward. The incident is told only as a legal precedent.

04.actor: A man claiming to be from Shot Mishot, and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha
04.event: A man said he was from Shot Mishot, and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha stood up and said that the place lies between the rivers.
04.turn: The Gemara asks why that matters and explains it bears on lineage status.
04.outcome: The incident leads into a discussion of where the area between the rivers lies. The man's fate is not told.
04.summary: A man told the Sages he came from Shot Mishot. Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha stood up and said the place lies between the Tigris and Euphrates. The Gemara then explains this matters for lineage, but never says what became of the man.
04.missing: What happened to the man and whether his claim was accepted. The passage turns into a geography and lineage discussion.

05.event: Walking on the road behind a woman, Rav told Rav Yehuda to hurry away from Gehenna so they would not be secluded with her.
05.turn: Rav Yehuda objected that Rav had permitted this for men of good morals.
05.outcome: Rav explained that he meant only men like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi and his colleagues, not ordinary men like themselves.
05.summary: Rav and Rav Yehuda were walking on the road with a woman ahead of them. Rav urged Rav Yehuda to quicken his pace so they would avoid being secluded with her. Rav Yehuda pointed out that Rav himself allowed this for men of good morals. Rav answered that only exceptional men like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi qualify, not the two of them.

06.actor: A groom and his bride, and Rabban Gamliel the Elder
06.event: A man told Rabban Gamliel he found no blood on his wedding night, and his bride said she was from the Dorketi family, who have no such blood.
06.turn: Rabban Gamliel checked her relatives and found her claim was true.
06.outcome: He told the groom to take possession of his acquisition and called him fortunate to have married into the Dorketi family.
06.summary: A man came to Rabban Gamliel the Elder saying he found no blood on his wedding night. His bride said she was from the Dorketi family, whose women have no such blood. Rabban Gamliel questioned her relatives and found it true, then told the groom to keep his bride and called him fortunate.

07.actor: A woman and the child she carried to Jerusalem
07.event: A woman came to Jerusalem with a child on her shoulders, raised him, and he later had intercourse with her.
07.turn: They were brought to court, where it was not certain he was her son.
07.outcome: They were stoned because he clung to her, which gave him the presumptive status of her son.
07.summary: A woman arrived in Jerusalem carrying a child on her shoulders, and she raised him. When he grew up he had intercourse with her. The court stoned both, not because he was definitely her son, but because he had clung to her like a son.

08.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya and a heretic
08.event: A heretic mocked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya as a man of thorns, citing a verse that calls the best of Israel a brier.
08.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua called him a fool and pointed to the end of the verse.
08.outcome: He gave two readings of the verse that turn the insult into praise.
08.summary: A heretic insulted Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya by quoting a verse that says the best of them is like a brier. Rabbi Yehoshua called him a fool and sent him to the end of the verse. He then explained that the thorns protect a breach, and that the righteous grind the nations down.
08.missing: The heretic's reaction. The exchange ends with Rabbi Yehoshua's reply.

09.actor: Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of Dabil, and Shmuel
09.event: Rav Yosef acted in accordance with Rav's opinion, and Shmuel took offense and sarcastically remarked on the Sage's wisdom.
09.turn: The Gemara uses Shmuel's anger to prove Rav and Shmuel really disagreed, then suggests Rav Yosef's case may have involved a daughter who denied her father's right.
09.outcome: The Gemara concludes that Rav Yosef must have ruled in the case where she did not deny, which explains why Shmuel took exception.
09.summary: Rav Yosef issued a ruling following Rav's view about a betrothal. Shmuel took offense and sarcastically asked whether wisdom is measured in a large measure only for this Sage. The Gemara uses that reaction as a legal argument about whether Rav and Shmuel truly disagreed.
09.missing: The details of the case Rav Yosef decided and any outcome for the parties. The incident is used only as evidence in an argument.

10.event: The two schools disagreed for two and a half years over whether it would have been better for man not to have been created.
10.outcome: They concluded it would have been better had man not been created, but now that he has been, he should examine his actions.
10.summary: For two and a half years Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel argued over whether man should have been created. In the end they took a vote and decided it would have been better for man not to have been created. Since he has been, he should examine or scrutinize his deeds.
10.missing: Who spoke or what particular events occurred. It is a summary of a long dispute and its resolution, not a told scene.

11.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi (Rabbi), on his deathbed
11.event: Rabbi, near death, called in his sons and then the Sages of Israel and gave instructions for his household, his burial and his succession.
11.turn: His wishes were later interpreted in light of events: he kept coming home on Shabbat eves until a neighbor knocked and he stopped, and the two attendants he named died before him.
11.outcome: The instructions were followed: Gamliel became Nasi, he was eulogized in the cities, and the study sessions were to resume after thirty days.
11.summary: On his deathbed Rabbi told his sons to honor their stepmother and to keep his lamp, table and bed in place, and he named two attendants to serve him in death. Each Shabbat eve he kept coming home, until a neighbor knocked and his maidservant said he was sitting inside, after which he never came again. He then told the Sages not to eulogize him in the small towns, to resume study after thirty days, and that Gamliel should be Nasi and Hanina bar Hama should head the yeshiva. The attendants died before him, and the people understood the instructions in the light of events.

12.event: Rabbi Akiva collected an etrog on the first of Shevat and separated two tithes from it, one by Beit Shammai's view and one by Beit Hillel's.
12.turn: Rav Mesharshiyya cites it as proof that Beit Shammai acted on their own opinion.
12.outcome: The outcome is not in the passage.
12.summary: Rabbi Akiva once picked an etrog on the first of Shevat and tithed it twice, as though it belonged to two different tithing years. This is cited as an objection to the claim that Beit Shammai did not act on their own view.
12.missing: The rest of the incident and its resolution. It is cited only as a legal objection.

13.actor: A woman holding a bag of documents, the deceased's heirs, and Rav Nachman
13.event: Heirs demanded a bag of documents deposited with a woman, who said she had seized it from the deceased while he was alive.
13.turn: Rav Nachman asked for witnesses that the deceased had claimed it from her while alive, and she had none.
13.outcome: He ruled her seizure counted as seizing after death, which is worth nothing.
13.summary: A woman had a bag of documents deposited with her, and the dead man's heirs came to claim it. She said she had seized it from him while he was alive, to recover a debt. Rav Nachman asked for witnesses, and she had none, so he ruled it was seizure after death and invalid.

14.actor: The daughter-in-law of the house of the son of Elyashiv, the orphans, and Ravina
14.event: She claimed her marriage contract from the orphans, who found it embarrassing that she appeared in house clothes.
14.turn: She went and dressed in all her clothes, and the case came before Ravina.
14.outcome: Ravina ruled, following Rav, that a widow's clothes are appraised and counted in the payment.
14.summary: A widow was taking the orphans to court to collect her marriage contract. They told her it was demeaning for her to appear in house clothes. She dressed in all her finery, and when they came before Ravina he ruled that the court values what a widow is wearing and counts it against her payment.

15.actor: Reish Lakish, Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar
15.event: A case about a man's priestly status came before Rabbi Yochanan, with Reish Lakish and Rabbi Elazar sitting there, and Reish Lakish asked whether the man had received a share at the threshing floor.
15.turn: Rabbi Yochanan answered with the same line Rabbi Elazar had used earlier, that the priesthood does not cease where there is no threshing floor.
15.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not saying earlier that the ruling came from Rabbi Yochanan.
15.summary: Earlier Reish Lakish challenged a man's priestly status and Rabbi Elazar replied with a rebuttal. Later, with all three sitting before Rabbi Yochanan, a similar case arose, and Reish Lakish raised the same question. Rabbi Yochanan gave Rabbi Elazar's same reply, so Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar for not saying it had come from Rabbi Yochanan.

16.event: The Sages suggested asking Mar Ukva's court in Kafrei, then reversed the names of the opinions and sent the question to Rav.
16.turn: Rav swore that she needs both a bill of divorce and refusal and said Shmuel would never say otherwise.
16.outcome: Rav's oath shows the opinion was wrongly attributed to Shmuel.
16.summary: Shmuel's ruling on a minor betrothed without her father's consent was challenged, and the Sages swapped the names and sent the question to Rav. Rav swore that she needs both a divorce and refusal, and that Shmuel would never say otherwise.
16.missing: Who the Sages speaking were, who asked, and what happened after Rav's answer.

17.actor: Bunyam ben Nunyam and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
17.event: Bunyam ben Nunyam sent Rabbi a gift of fine linens.
17.turn: The Gemara notes the linens folded to the size of a nut.
17.outcome: The gift is described, but no response or consequence follows.
17.summary: A wealthy man named Bunyam ben Nunyam once sent Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi a gift of four kinds of fine linen. They were so thin that they folded down to the size of a nut or pistachio and unfolded large enough to cover Rabbi's body.
17.missing: Any reaction from Rabbi and the circumstances of the gift. The passage serves to explain a word.

18.event: A man came before Rav Yosef about a daughter's support, and Rav Yosef told the heirs to give her dates from the mats.
18.turn: Abaye objected that not even a creditor could collect from movable property.
18.outcome: Rav Yosef explained he meant dates still attached and ripe for plucking, which are not movable property.
18.summary: Someone brought a case about a daughter's support to Rav Yosef, who ruled she should be given dates lying on mats. Abaye objected that even a creditor could not collect that way. Rav Yosef replied that he meant ripe dates still on the tree.
18.missing: Who the person was and what finally happened to the daughter.

19.actor: Rabbi Meir, and a man who fell into the Great Cistern
19.event: Rabbi Meir cited an incident of a man who fell into the Great Cistern and emerged after three days.
19.turn: The Sages told Rabbi Meir that one does not cite miraculous events.
19.outcome: The rest is a debate over what made it miraculous.
19.summary: Rabbi Meir cited an incident of a man who fell into the Great Cistern and survived three days. The Sages objected that miraculous events are not used for general rulings. The Gemara then debates what exactly would have been miraculous.
19.missing: The details of the man's fall and rescue, which the passage only alludes to.

20.actor: Rav Huna and his son Rabba
20.event: Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son Rabba to see whether Rabba would get angry.
20.turn: The Gemara asks whether the test might have made Rabba sin, then explains Rav Huna had forgone his honor.
20.outcome: The incident is accepted as legitimate, with the tear made at the seam and at a moment when Rabba was already angry.
20.summary: Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son Rabba to see whether he would become angry. The Gemara asks whether this would make his son sin, and answers that Rav Huna had forgone his honor. It adds that he tore at the seam, and did so when Rabba was already angry for another reason.
